q: In the SPARROW memory aid for documents required on board, what does the 'O' stand for?
a: Operating limitations: AFM/POH, supplements, placards, markings
d: Owner's maintenance records: airframe, engine and propeller logbooks
Overhaul records: engine and propeller time since overhaul
Operating checklist: normal and emergency checklists
why: SPARROW = Supplements, Placards, Airworthiness certificate, Registration, Radio station license (if required), Operating limitations, Weight and balance. The operating limitations come from the AFM/POH, its supplements, placards and markings (14 CFR 91.9). Logbooks are maintenance records and are not on the required-on-board list.

q: When does a U.S.-registered airplane need an FCC radio station license on board?
a: Only when it is operated outside the United States
d: Whenever any transmitting radio is installed
Only when it is operated under IFR
Only when it is used for hire or flight instruction
why: The OEG lists the radio station license as required only for operations outside the U.S., an FCC rule (47 CFR 87.18). Domestic flights don't need one even with radios installed.

q: On preflight you find the airworthiness certificate displayed but no registration certificate anywhere in the aircraft. May you fly it?
a: No; 14 CFR 91.203 requires the registration certificate on board
d: Yes; the registration is already on file with the FAA registry
Yes, but only for day VFR flights that stay in the local area
Yes; 14 CFR 91.203 requires only the airworthiness certificate
why: 14 CFR 91.203 requires both the airworthiness certificate and the registration certificate to be in the aircraft. A record at the FAA registry does not substitute for the certificate on board.

q: Besides the SPARROW documents, which item does the OEG list as required in the aircraft?
a: A magnetic compass deviation card
d: The airframe and engine logbooks
A copy of the Type Certificate Data Sheet
The pilot's logbook with flight review endorsement
why: The OEG adds the compass deviation card (14 CFR 23.1547) and the external data plate/serial number (14 CFR 45.11) to the SPARROW documents. The logbooks and the TCDS are not on that list.

q: How recently must the VOR equipment have been checked for it to be used under IFR?
a: Within the preceding 30 days
d: Within the preceding 10 days
Within the preceding 90 days
Within the preceding 24 calendar months
why: 14 CFR 91.171 requires a VOR accuracy check within the preceding 30 days for IFR use. 24 calendar months is the interval for the altimeter/static system and transponder checks.

q: For IFR flight, how often must the altimeter, altitude reporting equipment and static system be tested and inspected?
a: Every 24 calendar months
d: Every 12 calendar months
Every 100 hours of time in service
Every 30 days, by a pilot ground check
why: 14 CFR 91.411 sets a 24-calendar-month test of the altimeter, encoder and static system for IFR. The transponder (14 CFR 91.413) is also on a 24-calendar-month cycle.

q: How often must an ELT's operation and battery condition be inspected under 14 CFR 91.207?
a: Every 12 calendar months
d: Every 24 calendar months
Every 100 hours of time in service
Every 6 calendar months
why: The OEG's inspection list includes an ELT check of operation and battery condition every 12 calendar months (14 CFR 91.207). 24 calendar months is the altimeter/static and transponder interval.

q: An annual inspection was signed off on March 10, 2025. With no new annual, through what date may the airplane be flown?
a: March 31, 2026
d: March 10, 2026
February 28, 2026
March 31, 2027
why: The annual must be within the preceding 12 calendar months (14 CFR 91.409), so it runs to the end of the same month one year later.

q: A flight school's twin is used for its multi-engine training, flown with the school's own instructors. What inspection does this use add to the annual?
a: A 100-hour inspection
d: A 50-hour inspection
A 200-hour inspection
A second annual every 6 months
why: An aircraft used for hire, or for flight instruction for hire in an aircraft the instructor provides, needs a 100-hour inspection in addition to the annual (14 CFR 91.409).

q: You own a twin and hire a freelance CFI, who brings no aircraft, to train you in it. Does your twin need a 100-hour inspection?
a: No; the 100-hour applies when the instructor provides the aircraft
d: Yes; any flight instruction given for hire requires a 100-hour inspection
Yes; every multi-engine airplane needs a 100-hour inspection
No, but only if its annual was done within the last 6 months
why: The OEG ties the 100-hour to use for hire or to flight instruction in an aircraft the CFI provides (14 CFR 91.409). When the student supplies the airplane, the annual and other applicable checks are what's required.

q: During the oral, where would you show the examiner that ADs and life-limited parts have been complied with?
a: In the airframe and engine logbooks
d: In the Limitations section of the POH
On the back of the airworthiness certificate
On the equipment list in the AFM
why: AD and life-limited part compliance is recorded in the maintenance records (14 CFR 91.403, 91.417). The OEG suggests tabbing those logbook pages and making a status sheet showing when each item comes due.

q: Part 91 allows operation with certain inoperative equipment by which two methods?
a: An approved MEL (91.213(a)), or the no-MEL procedure of 91.213(d)
d: A special flight permit, or an FAA Form 337 field approval
The KOEL alone, or an INOP placard approved by the pilot in command
The POH emergency checklist, or a waiver obtained from ATC
why: 14 CFR 91.213 lets inoperative items that aren't essential for safe flight be deferred either with an FAA-approved MEL or, with no MEL, by the 91.213(d) procedure. The OEG notes many applicants are weak on this rule.

q: You discover inoperative equipment during preflight. Which three choices does the OEG give you?
a: Cancel the flight, get maintenance before flight, or defer the item
d: Defer the item, notify ATC, or limit the flight to day VFR
Cancel the flight, fly with a placard, or file an ASRS report
Get maintenance, obtain a special flight permit, or fly the airplane as is
why: For items found during preflight or before departure, the decision is to cancel, obtain maintenance before flight, or defer the item using the MEL or 91.213(d).

q: In cruise, the landing light circuit breaker pops and won't reset. How does the 91.213(d) deferral process apply?
a: It doesn't apply in flight; follow the POH/AFM procedures
d: Placard the switch INOP in flight and continue normally
Write a deferral entry in flight, then continue the flight
Declare an emergency; the airplane is now unairworthy
why: Deferral under an MEL or 91.213(d) is a preflight tool for items found before departure. A failure that happens in flight is handled with the POH/AFM procedures.

q: No MEL. Preflight reveals an inoperative item that an airworthiness directive requires to be operational. What is the airplane's status?
a: Not airworthy; maintenance is required before flight
d: Airworthy once the item is placarded INOPERATIVE
Airworthy for day VFR, but not for night or IFR
Airworthy if the pilot writes it up in the squawk log
why: If the item is required by regulation for the flight, by the type certification or equipment list/KOEL, or by an AD, the airplane is unairworthy and needs maintenance. Placarding only works for items nothing requires.

q: An inoperative item turns out to be something you may repair as preventive maintenance. Per the OEG, how is the airplane returned to service?
a: The pilot may fix it and record the work in the maintenance records
d: The pilot may fix it, but an A&P mechanic must sign the return to service
The pilot fixes it; preventive maintenance needs no record
Only a mechanic holding an IA may approve the repair
why: Preventive maintenance (14 CFR Part 43 Appendix A) may be done by a certificated pilot on an aircraft they own or operate, but the work must be logged. The OEG says the pilot may then return the airplane to airworthy condition.

q: An FAA-approved MEL for a Part 91 airplane applies to which aircraft?
a: One specific aircraft, by serial and registration number
d: Every aircraft of that make and model, in any operator's fleet
Any aircraft that is listed in the operator's fleet
Any aircraft that the MEL holder happens to be flying
why: An approved MEL is tied to one airframe, identified by its serial and registration numbers. The master MEL (MMEL) for the make and model is only its basis, not authority to operate.

q: An inoperative item does not appear anywhere in the aircraft's approved MEL. How should you treat it?
a: As required equipment that must be working
d: As optional equipment, deferrable at pilot discretion
As deferrable once a mechanic signs a logbook entry
As allowed to be inoperative for day VFR flight
why: An MEL works as a list of permissions: only the items listed, under their stated conditions, may be inoperative. Anything outside the list or its conditions must be operational.

q: What is the difference between an MEL and the aircraft's equipment list?
a: The MEL says what may be inop; the equipment list shows what's installed
d: They are one document, filed under two different names in the AFM
The equipment list says what may be inop; the MEL shows what's installed
The MEL covers only the avionics; the equipment list covers the rest
why: The OEG warns not to confuse them. The equipment list (in the AFM) records installed equipment and marks some items required; the MEL is an FAA-approved authorization to fly with specific items inoperative.

q: With an approved MEL, you find the position lights inoperative before a day flight. Which sequence is correct?
a: Record it, repair or defer per MEL, switch OFF, open CB, placard INOP
d: Placard INOP, fly the day flight, then record it after landing
Open the CB, fly day VFR, then have maintenance check the MEL
Defer per MEL, fly the day flight, then make the maintenance record entry
why: The OEG sequence: enter the discrepancy in the maintenance record, repair or defer under the MEL, then (once day flight is confirmed allowed) leave the switch OFF, open the circuit breaker or follow the procedures document, and placard the switch INOPERATIVE.

q: What FAA document authorizes a Part 91 operator to use an MEL for a specific aircraft?
a: A Letter of Authorization (LOA)
d: A special flight permit
An FAA Form 337 field approval
An amended Type Certificate Data Sheet
why: Once the operator requests an MEL and the FAA issues an LOA, the MEL applies to that aircraft and becomes mandatory.

q: After the FAA issues an LOA for an aircraft's MEL, may the owner defer an item under 91.213(d) instead?
a: No; the MEL becomes mandatory for that aircraft
d: Yes; the pilot may pick either method on any flight
Yes, but only for flights conducted in day VFR
Yes, if a mechanic agrees and signs the logbook
why: Once the LOA is issued the MEL is mandatory, and every deferral must follow its terms and the operator's procedures document.

q: How does the FAA regard an approved MEL issued to a small Part 91 airplane?
a: As an STC for that aircraft, by serial and registration number
d: As an advisory guide that the pilot in command may set aside
As an amendment to the type certificate for that whole model
As a temporary airworthiness certificate for that aircraft
why: The OEG says the FAA treats an approved MEL as a supplemental type certificate tied to one aircraft's serial and registration numbers, not to the whole model.

q: Which inoperative equipment may a pilot deactivate without help from a maintenance provider?
a: Items an MEL or KOEL allows inop, or preventive maintenance items
d: Any item at all, as long as it is then placarded INOPERATIVE
Any item, provided the pilot holds a commercial certificate
Only items that are specifically listed on the Type Certificate Data Sheet
why: Per the OEG, other deactivations need a maintenance provider to decide whether the aircraft remains airworthy, disable or remove the item, placard it and make the logbook entry.
src: OEG 1A-9 · FAA-H-8083-25, 14 CFR Part 43 App A

q: Per the OEG, 'deactivating' an inoperative item consists of what?
a: Disabling it, placarding it, and making a maintenance log entry
d: Removing it, re-weighing the airplane, and filing a Form 337
Pulling its breaker and briefing the next pilot verbally
Placarding it and noting it in the flight plan remarks
why: Deactivation means disabling the item, placarding it inoperative, and recording it in the maintenance logs. If it involves maintenance, it must be done and recorded under Part 43.

q: A pilot with ASEL and AMEL ratings did a flight review in a Cessna 172 fourteen months ago. Does it satisfy 61.56 for flying a twin?
a: Yes; it may be in any aircraft the pilot is rated in
d: No; a separate flight review is needed in each class
No; multi-engine pilots need a review every 12 months
Yes, but only if the review included engine-out tasks
why: 14 CFR 61.56 requires a flight review every 24 calendar months in an aircraft for which the pilot is rated; one review in either class covers both. Alternating classes is good practice, not a rule.

q: A pilot's only recent landings are three in a Piper Seminole last month. May they carry passengers in a Cessna 172?
a: No; single- and multi-engine land are different classes
d: Yes; the twin is more complex, so its landings count
Yes, provided all three landings were to a full stop
Yes, because both airplanes are in the same category
why: 14 CFR 61.57 requires three takeoffs and landings within 90 days in the same category, class and type (if a type rating is required). Twin landings don't count toward single-engine currency.

q: A type-rated pilot made three takeoffs and landings in a Boeing 777 last week. Do they count for carrying passengers in a Baron?
a: Yes; same category and class, and the Baron needs no type rating
d: No; the landings must be in the same make and model
No; turbine-airplane landings don't count for pistons
No; type-rated aircraft count only for other type-rated aircraft
why: Both are airplane multi-engine land. The type requirement applies only when the airplane being flown requires a type rating, which the Baron doesn't.

q: A pilot holding a 777 type rating made three landings in a Baron last week. May they now carry passengers in a 777?
a: No; the 777 needs the landings in the same type
d: Yes; both are multi-engine land airplanes
Yes, because the pilot holds a current 777 type rating
Yes, provided the Baron landings were made at night
why: For an aircraft that requires a type rating, passenger-carrying currency must be in that type (14 CFR 61.57). Currency flows from the 777 to the Baron, not the other way.

q: To carry passengers at night in a light twin, what recent experience does 14 CFR 61.57 require?
a: Three takeoffs and landings at night in a multi-engine airplane within 90 days
d: Three takeoffs and landings at night in any airplane within 90 days
Three takeoffs and landings at night in a twin within 6 calendar months
One takeoff and landing at night in a multi-engine airplane within 90 days
why: Passenger currency is three takeoffs and landings in the preceding 90 days in the same category and class, done at night if the flight is at night (61.57(b) also requires the night landings to be to a full stop). Single-engine landings don't count for the twin.

q: A multi-engine, instrument-rated pilot met all instrument currency in a single-engine airplane. May they fly IFR in a twin?
a: Yes; instrument currency is by category (airplane), not class
d: No; the approaches must be flown in a multi-engine airplane
No; an instrument proficiency check in a twin is required
Yes, but only after flying three IFR approaches in the twin
why: 14 CFR 61.57 instrument experience must be in an airplane, powered-lift, helicopter or airship as appropriate, or an appropriately certificated simulator. None of it needs to be done in a twin.

q: Which FAA program lets a pilot select multi-engine proficiency tasks and document them, going beyond basic currency?
a: The FAA WINGS Pilot Proficiency Program
d: The Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS)
The BasicMed online recurrent medical course
The Part 141 school stage-check program
why: The OEG suggests practicing ACS tasks, flying with a proficient instructor more often than the 24-month flight review, and completing WINGS tasks documented through the FAA Safety Program.

q: Below what altitude does the OEG say simulated engine failures should be reserved for simulators and training devices?
a: 200 feet AGL
d: 400 feet AGL
500 feet AGL
1,000 feet AGL
why: Simulated failures below 400 ft AGL call for extreme caution, and those below 200 ft AGL belong in simulators; a low-altitude engine failure isn't worth the risk in the airplane.

q: According to the OEG, how should simulated engine failures below 3,000 feet AGL be introduced?
a: By smoothly retarding the throttle
d: By moving the mixture to idle cutoff
By turning the fuel selector OFF
By switching off the engine's magnetos
why: Using the throttle keeps the engine running so power can be restored at once. Cutting fuel or ignition close to the ground risks a real failure with no time to recover.

q: When are unannounced simulated engine failures appropriate in multi-engine flying, per the OEG?
a: Only for testing or checking, agreed on before the flight
d: On any training flight, to build realistic reactions
Whenever the airplane is above 3,000 feet AGL
Only in the traffic pattern, where real failures occur
why: Simulated failures should be briefed in advance, including how they'll be introduced and the expected response. Surprise failures are only for testing and checking, agreed on before the flight.

q: Besides engine failures, what other practice does the OEG recommend to reduce multi-engine training risk?
a: Systems failures, including partial-panel instrument work
d: Engine failures close to the ground, below 200 feet AGL
Unannounced engine cuts on short final approach
Vmc demonstrations at low altitude near the airport
why: The OEG stresses that systems knowledge is critically important and recommends practicing systems failures and partial-panel flying. It specifically warns against low-altitude and unbriefed engine failures.

q: Per the OEG's risk-mitigation guidance, what should you avoid doing on the runway after landing?
a: Changing the airplane's configuration without a clear need
d: Using differential braking for directional control
Holding aileron into the wind during the rollout
Leaving the flaps extended until the airplane is clear of the runway
why: Reaching for flaps or other controls during the rollout invites grabbing the wrong one, such as the gear selector. Leave the configuration alone until clear unless there's a clear operational need.

q: During normal taxi in a light twin, what is the primary means of steering?
a: The steerable nosewheel
d: Differential engine power
Differential braking
Rudder deflection in the propwash
why: Steering is done mainly with the steerable nosewheel. Differential power can help if needed, and brakes and throttles control momentum.

q: Per the OEG, how should taxi speed be controlled in a light twin?
a: With throttles and brakes, keeping power low to avoid riding brakes
d: With steady light braking held against a moderate power setting
With differential power as the main means of speed control
With nosewheel steering and rudder alone, without the brakes
why: Keep power low so you aren't dragging the brakes, and use throttles and brakes together to manage speed. A heavier twin carries more momentum and takes longer to stop, so plan ahead.

q: Using differential power to tighten a right turn while taxiing, what do you do?
a: Reduce right engine power, add left engine power, use right rudder/brake
d: Add right engine power, reduce left engine power, use right rudder/brake
Reduce both engines to idle and use the right brake alone
Add left engine power, reduce right, and hold left rudder/brake
why: More thrust on the left and less on the right yaws the nose right, helping the turn along with right rudder and brake.

q: Taxiing with a strong crosswind from the left, which engine gets more power to help hold direction?
a: The left (upwind) engine, turning the nose away from the wind
d: The right (downwind) engine, turning the nose into the wind
Both engines equally, using brakes alone for direction
The right engine, to counter the left-turning tendency
why: A crosswind makes the airplane weathervane into the wind. Extra power on the upwind engine creates a turning moment away from the wind to counter it.

q: Why does the OEG warn against very sharp taxi turns using brakes and differential power?
a: It can pivot on a stationary inboard wheel, overstressing the gear
d: Differential power can overheat the inboard engine's cylinders
Sharp turns can let the propeller tips contact the ground
It can unlatch the nosewheel steering and jam it off-center
why: Pivoting about a stationary inboard wheel puts loads on the landing gear it wasn't designed for.

q: An engine fails during a critical phase of flight. How does the OEG say the checklist should be used?
a: Do the memorized action items first, then verify with the checklist
d: Read each item from the printed checklist before taking any action
Skip the checklist entirely until the airplane is on the ground
Use the checklist only if the failed engine can't be restarted
why: Time-critical items are flown from memory; once things settle, the written checklist is used to confirm each action. A checklist can be done-then-verify rather than read-and-do, but one is always used.

q: Which is one reason the OEG gives for multi-engine training carrying greater risk?
a: Much more training time goes to emergency and engine-out procedures
d: Light twins are required to be flown by a two-pilot crew
Multi-engine airplanes are inherently less stable in pitch
Twins have fewer redundant systems than single-engine airplanes
why: The OEG also cites heavier, faster airplanes with complex systems, more planning and skill required, higher workload (worse if not current), and emergencies that can deteriorate much faster than in a single.

q: Fixation is the situational-awareness trap the OEG links to which factor?
a: Troubleshooting an equipment malfunction
d: Depending on advanced avionics
Handling a high workload
Lacking aircraft knowledge and experience
why: The OEG pairs high workload with task saturation, malfunctions with fixation while troubleshooting, lack of knowledge with confusion, and avionics dependency with complacency and inattention. Distractions and interruptions are the fifth factor.

q: What are the three most critical phases of flight in a multi-engine airplane, per the OEG?
a: Takeoff, initial climb, and landing
d: Taxi, takeoff, and landing
Takeoff, cruise, and approach
En route climb, descent, and go-around
why: Takeoff and initial climb put the airplane low, slow and at its heaviest weight; landing is also slow and close to the ground, so there is little margin.

q: Why does the OEG recommend starting the before-landing checklist early in a twin?
a: Patterns and approaches are flown faster than in most singles
d: The landing gear takes several minutes to extend
ATC requires it before you enter the traffic pattern
The checklist must be read twice in a multi-engine airplane
why: Higher pattern and approach speeds leave less time, so an early start on the checklist gives room to plan, set up spacing and stay ahead of the airplane.

q: In a typical light twin, what is the pilot's first priority during the takeoff roll, per the OEG?
a: Reaching at least Vmc + 5 knots before liftoff
d: Reaching Vyse before the nosewheel lifts off
Lifting off as early as possible to save runway
Reaching Vx before liftoff to clear obstacles
why: Below Vmc, directional control after an engine failure may be impossible unless power on the good engine is cut right away; the rudder can't counter the asymmetric yaw. The second priority is reaching Vy quickly.

q: After liftoff with both engines running, what is the multi-engine pilot's second priority, per the OEG?
a: Reaching Vy in the least amount of time
d: Holding Vx until reaching pattern altitude
Reaching cruise-climb airspeed immediately
Holding Vmc + 5 until reaching 400 feet AGL
why: Vy gives the greatest rate of climb with both engines operating, gaining altitude quickly. If an engine then fails, Vyse is held.

q: If an engine fails after takeoff, why does the OEG say to hold Vyse?
a: It gives the best OEI climb rate, or the least sink
d: It is the lowest speed with full rudder authority
It gives the most altitude per distance with OEI
It is the minimum speed for intentional engine cuts
why: With the dead engine feathered and a slight bank into the good engine, Vyse yields the most climb per minute, or the least sink if the airplane can't climb. Most gain per distance is Vxse; intentional cuts are at or above Vsse.

q: If the manufacturer publishes no rotation speed, what minimum Vr does the OEG suggest for a light twin?
a: Vmc + 5 knots
d: Vmc (red line)
Vyse (blue line)
1.3 Vso
why: Use the published Vr or Vlof when given; otherwise use at least Vmc + 5 knots. As a rule, light twins shouldn't be airborne before Vmc.

q: If climbing at Vy after takeoff would need a very steep nose-up attitude, what does the OEG recommend?
a: Limit the initial pitch attitude to 15 degrees
d: Limit the initial pitch attitude to 10 degrees
Limit the initial pitch attitude to 20 degrees
Climb at Vx instead until reaching 400 feet AGL
why: A pitch attitude above about 15 degrees would make control difficult if an engine quits, so the OEG suggests capping initial pitch at 15 degrees.

q: On a normal multi-engine departure, Vy is held until reaching what, per the OEG?
a: A safe single-engine maneuvering altitude, usually 400+ ft AGL
d: Traffic pattern altitude, typically 1,000 feet AGL
The single-engine service ceiling for the day's conditions
A safe gear-retraction height, typically 200 feet AGL
why: Right after takeoff, altitude is the priority over an en route climb speed. Vy is held until reaching a height, typically at least 400 ft AGL, from which single-engine maneuvering is safe.

q: Normally, when should the landing gear be retracted after a multi-engine takeoff?
a: Positive rate of climb and too little runway left to land
d: As soon as the main wheels have left the runway surface
Upon reaching Vy and an altitude of 400 feet AGL
Upon reaching Vyse, regardless of how much runway remains
why: Keep the gear down while a landing straight ahead on the remaining runway or overrun is still possible, and raise it once a positive rate of climb shows on the altimeter.

q: Departing a 9,000-ft runway at an airport 5,000 ft MSL, why not keep the gear down until the runway is used up?
a: It would give up climb performance and acceleration for too long
d: The gear extension speed limit is lower at high-altitude airports
The gear takes much longer to retract in thin, high-altitude air
Regulations require retraction before passing the departure end
why: On a very long runway, waiting until the end to raise the gear costs climb and acceleration for little benefit. The extra drag hurts even more in thin, high-density-altitude air.

q: Why might waiting for a positive rate of climb before raising the gear be impractical at a high-density-altitude airport?
a: Some twins can't climb at all there with the gear down
d: The altimeter lags too much at high density altitude
Gear retraction is prohibited above a set density altitude
The gear may fail to lock up in thin air
why: At high density altitude some twins have so little excess power that gear drag alone prevents a climb, so waiting for a positive rate on the altimeter could mean waiting indefinitely.

q: No approach speed is published. Per the OEG, what is the minimum final approach speed in a twin?
a: Vyse until short final with landing assured, never below Vmc
d: Vref (1.3 Vso) from the final approach fix all the way to the flare
Vxse until over the threshold, but never below Vsse
Vmc + 5 knots until short final, but never below Vso
why: Staying at or above Vyse until the landing is assured keeps the best single-engine performance available for a go-around; the airplane should never be slower than Vmc.
drop_reason: duplicate of o6-055 (same question and answer); its 'Vref (1.3 Vso)' distractor also matches the ACS no-published-speed approach standard in o8-010

q: No MEL. What is the first question in the OEG's 91.213(d) decision sequence for inoperative equipment?
a: Is the item part of the VFR-day type certification requirements?
d: Is the item required to be working by an airworthiness directive?
Is the item required by 14 CFR 91.205 for the planned flight?
Can the item be deactivated and placarded inoperative?
why: The order is: (1) VFR-day type certification, (2) 'Required' on the equipment list or KOEL, (3) 91.205 or other Part 91 rules, (4) an AD. Any yes means unairworthy. Then remove or deactivate and placard, and a pilot or mechanic decides it's not a hazard.

q: Where can you generally find the equipment required by an airplane's certification regulations?
a: The aircraft's equipment list and Type Certificate Data Sheet
d: The airworthiness certificate and the registration certificate
14 CFR 91.205 and the Aeronautical Information Manual
The pilot's checklist and the placards in the cockpit
why: Checking the certification rules (Part 23, or CAR 3 for much older aircraft) directly is complex; the OEG points to the equipment list and TCDS instead. 91.205 lists equipment for kinds of operation, which is a separate step.

q: Which kinds of operation does a typical kinds of operations equipment list (KOEL) address?
a: VFR day, VFR night, IFR day, IFR night, and icing
d: Normal, utility, acrobatic, and commuter categories
Part 91, Part 135, and Part 121 operations
Day, night, mountain, and overwater operations
why: The KOEL shows required equipment for each kind of operation the airplane is approved for. The equipment list and KOEL are in the AFM; an item marked 'Required' for the planned operation makes the airplane unairworthy if it's inoperative.

q: No MEL. You plan a night VFR flight and find the position lights inoperative. What applies?
a: It isn't airworthy for that flight until they're repaired
d: Placard them INOP and fly; the strobes satisfy the rule
Deactivate and placard them; you may then fly at night
They aren't required under VFR, so no action is needed
why: Step 3 asks whether 91.205 or another Part 91 rule (such as 91.209, aircraft lights) requires the item for the kind of operation. Position lights are required at night, so they can't be deferred for a night flight.

q: In the no-MEL decision sequence, an inoperative ATC transponder would be checked against which Part 91 equipment rule?
why: The OEG lists 91.205 (VFR day, VFR night, IFR equipment), 91.207 (ELTs), 91.209 (aircraft lights) and 91.215 (ATC transponders). 91.211 covers supplemental oxygen.

q: No MEL. If no type certification rule, equipment list/KOEL, Part 91 rule or AD requires the inoperative item, what must happen before flight?
a: Remove or deactivate it, and placard it or its control
d: Nothing, as long as it isn't needed for the planned flight
Note it on the squawk sheet for the next annual
Obtain a special flight permit from the FSDO
why: 14 CFR 91.213(d)(3) requires the item to be removed (flight deck control placarded, logbook updated per 14 CFR 43.9) or deactivated and placarded 'Inoperative'. Deactivation that involves maintenance must be done and recorded under Part 43.

q: Under 91.213(d), who makes the final determination that an inoperative item is not a hazard for the planned flight?
a: A certificated, appropriately rated pilot or mechanic
d: An FAA aviation safety inspector at the local FSDO
The registered owner shown on the aircraft's registration
Only a mechanic holding an Inspection Authorization
why: The final step: a certificated, appropriately rated pilot or mechanic decides the inoperative item creates no hazard for the planned flight conditions (e.g., day VFR, night VFR).

q: Your airplane has an MEL. An inoperative item isn't in the MEL but is required by the type certification. What is the status?
a: Not airworthy; maintenance is required before flight
d: Airworthy if deferred under 91.213(d) instead
Airworthy once an 'O' procedure is done and it is placarded
Airworthy for day VFR flights, once placarded
why: The first MEL step asks whether the item is missing from the MEL but required by type certification, an AD or other special conditions. If so, it must be repaired; 91.213(d) is not an option once an MEL is in use.

q: In an MEL, what does an 'M' procedure mean?
a: Maintenance personnel must do it before operating with the item inop
d: The pilot may do it before or during operation with the item inop
It is a monitoring item the pilot checks before each flight
Maintenance must repair the item within the next 10 days
why: 'M' (maintenance) procedures must be done by maintenance personnel before operation begins. 'O' (operations) procedures can be done by the pilot, before or during operation with the item inoperative.

q: Under an MEL, after the O or M procedure is done, what are the remaining steps?
a: Placard it, update the logbook, and confirm it poses no hazard
d: Obtain a new LOA from the FAA, then placard the item
Notify the local FSDO by phone, then fly only the next scheduled flight
Update the logbook; placards are not used with an MEL
why: The OEG's MEL sequence: (1) check it isn't required outside the MEL, (2) do the O or M procedure, (3) placard and update the maintenance record, (4) the pilot confirms it doesn't create a hazard for the flight conditions.

q: In the OEG light-twin takeoff briefing, what is the plan if an engine fails before reaching Vmc or Vr?
a: Retard both throttles and abort the takeoff
d: Continue the takeoff and feather the failed engine
Rotate immediately and climb out at Vxse
Keep full power on the good engine and steer with rudder
why: Below Vmc the airplane can't be controlled with asymmetric thrust, and below Vr it isn't ready to fly, so the plan is to close both throttles and stop.
src: OEG 1C-7 · OEG App 4 · FAA Safety ALC-30

q: Per the OEG takeoff briefing, an engine fails after liftoff with the landing gear still down. What is the plan?
a: Close both throttles and land straight ahead
d: Raise the gear, feather, and climb at Vyse
Add full power and turn back to the runway
Feather the dead engine and climb at Vxse
why: Gear still down means runway remains to land on; closing both throttles and landing ahead avoids trying to climb out on one engine in a draggy configuration.
src: OEG 1C-7 · OEG App 4 · FAA Safety ALC-30
drop_reason: duplicate of o7-038 (engine fails after liftoff, gear down: close both throttles, land ahead); o7-038 has stronger distractors

q: An engine fails after liftoff with the gear retracted. What is the OEG briefing's order of actions?
a: Control, Configure, Climb, Checklist
d: Configure, Control, Checklist, Climb
Checklist, Control, Configure, Climb
Control, Climb, Checklist, Configure
why: Control first (pitch and power for Vyse), then configure (flaps, gear, prop), then climb at Vyse with zero sideslip, and run the checklist at 400 ft AGL.
src: OEG 1C-7 · OEG App 4 · FAA Safety ALC-30
drop_reason: duplicate of o7-042 (control, configure, climb, checklist order); o7-042 has stronger distractors

q: What does the 'Configure' step of the OEG engine-out takeoff briefing include?
a: Flaps, gear, and propeller
d: Cowl flaps, trim, and fuel pumps
Mixtures, magnetos, and alternators
Lights, transponder, and radios
why: Configure means cleaning up drag: flaps and gear up, and the failed engine's prop feathered.
src: OEG 1C-7 · OEG App 4 · FAA Safety ALC-30

q: In the 'Climb' step after an engine failure on takeoff, what do you maintain?
a: Vyse with zero sideslip
d: Vy with the wings level
Vxse with the ball centered
Vmc with full rudder applied
why: Hold Vyse and fly zero sideslip (a small bank toward the operating engine) to minimize drag and get the best one-engine climb.
src: OEG 1C-7 · OEG App 4 · FAA Safety ALC-30

q: Per the OEG takeoff briefing, when is the checklist run after an engine failure with the gear up?
a: Upon reaching 400 feet AGL
d: Immediately, before any other action
Upon reaching 1,000 feet AGL
Only after returning to land
why: The memorized control, configure and climb actions come first; the written checklist is used once the airplane reaches 400 ft AGL.
src: OEG 1C-7 · OEG App 4 · FAA Safety ALC-30

q: Which distance, besides takeoff distance, is stated in the OEG light-twin takeoff briefing?
a: Accelerate-stop distance
d: Accelerate-go distance
Landing distance over a 50-ft obstacle
Balanced field length
why: The template covers density altitude, runway length, takeoff weight, takeoff distance, accelerate-stop distance, single-engine climb rate and service ceiling, and Vmc, Vr, Vyse and Vy.
src: OEG 1C-7 · OEG App 4 · FAA Safety ALC-30

q: In the OEG takeoff briefing, the gear-up branch (control, configure, climb, checklist) applies once airborne at or above what speed?
a: Vxse
d: Vmc
Vsse
Vr
why: The briefing splits failures by phase: below Vmc or Vr, abort; airborne with the gear down, close both throttles and land ahead; airborne at or above Vxse with the gear up, fly the POH/AFM engine-out procedure.
src: OEG 1C-7 · OEG App 4 · FAA Safety ALC-30

q: You plan a VFR flight through Class C airspace. How recently must the ATC transponder have been tested and inspected?
a: Within the preceding 24 calendar months
d: Within the preceding 12 calendar months
Within the last 100 hours of time in service
Within the preceding 30 days
why: 14 CFR 91.413 requires a transponder test and inspection within the preceding 24 calendar months for any use, VFR or IFR. 30 days is the IFR VOR check; 12 calendar months is the annual and ELT interval.

q: In the SPARROW list of documents required on board, what does the 'W' stand for?
a: Current weight and balance data
d: Current weather briefing record
Current pilot logbook and medical
Current airframe and engine logbooks
why: The OEG lists current weight and balance data (citing 14 CFR 23.2620) as the last SPARROW item. Maintenance logbooks, the pilot's logbook and a weather briefing record are not on the required-on-board list.

q: No MEL. The inoperative item is required by the aircraft's TCDS or was installed under an STC. Per the OEG, who must address it?
a: A maintenance provider, who decides if it can be made airworthy
d: The pilot, by placarding it INOPERATIVE and logging it
The pilot, as preventive maintenance under 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix A
The registered owner, by signing a logbook entry
why: Per OEG 1A-5, items tied to the type certificate data sheet, the factory equipment list or an STC go to a maintenance provider, who decides whether the airplane can be made airworthy and makes a logbook entry. Equipment nothing requires that won't be repaired is disabled, placarded inoperative and logged; an item the type certification requires can't be deferred this way (App 3).
